title: Error Highways: Scaling Predictive Coding to Very Deep Networks
setting: Very deep PC MLP/CNN networks; direct feedback pathways for the output error
what_it_shows: Shows per-layer error norms decay geometrically with depth under plain PC (attenuated by the inference step size at every layer), and fixes training by adding fixed random feedback ('highway') projections that inject the output error directly into every layer, bypassing sequential layer-to-layer propagation; compares against muPC.
why: Same diagnosis (error fails to reach lower layers with standard inference) but the remedy is architectural (skip/highway feedback connections), not precision reweighting, and not derived from any measured output-Jacobian spectral quantity; no transformer setting studied.

title: Closed-form predictive coding via hierarchical Gaussian filters
setting: PC networks reformulated as hierarchical Gaussian filters (HGFs); FashionMNIST-scale MLP, online/non-stationary learning
what_it_shows: Traces PC's depth-degradation directly to fixing the precision matrix to the identity, and restores precision-weighted message passing with precisions learned online as Bayesian (volatility-coupled) posterior beliefs at every layer jointly with weights and activations, closed-form (no iterative relaxation or backprop through time needed).
why: The closest single match to the claim's diagnosis: explicitly states that fixing precision to identity is the cause of PC's sharp depth-degradation, and that restoring learned, per-layer precision fixes it -- essentially confirming the claim's premise in different words. But the precision-setting RULE is categorically different: an HGF/Bayesian volatility-coupled posterior update, not a value computed from the output Jacobian's spectral norm lambda_max(J^T J), not re-measured as a quantity of network gain, and not block-wise for a transformer; study is small MLP, not deep transformers, and the paper does not report credit-cosine-to-BP or gradient-vanishing diagnostics the way the claim does.

title: Towards the Training of Deeper Predictive Coding Neural Networks
setting: Deep PC MLP/CNN classifiers (CIFAR-scale), depths up to ~tens of layers; standard activity-relaxation PC
what_it_shows: Diagnoses an energy/error imbalance across layers in deep PC networks that prevents training (closely matching the claim's 'error does not reach lower layers' diagnosis), and fixes it with hand-designed temporal/depth precision SCHEDULES applied to prediction errors (constant, linear-decay, exponential-decay, and a 'spiking' schedule that boosts precision at the currently-updating layer) rather than a precision value computed from any measured network quantity.
why: Anticipates both halves of the claim's premise (unit-precision PC fails to train deep nets because error does not propagate to lower layers) and the general remedy class (layer/time-varying precision weighting of errors). Differs sharply in mechanism: precision is a hand-tuned schedule indexed by relaxation step and layer, never measured from the output Jacobian or its spectral norm, and not re-measured during training; study is MLP/CNN, not transformers.

title: muPC: Scaling Predictive Coding to 100+ Layer Networks
setting: Very deep (100+ layer) MLP PC networks; studies the Hessian of the PC energy w.r.t. activities
what_it_shows: Explicitly computes the spectral properties (largest/smallest eigenvalues, condition number kappa = |lambda_max|/|lambda_min|) of the inference Hessian H_z at each layer and shows it blows up with depth, explaining why fixed-step PC inference fails to converge in deep nets; fixes this with a STATIC analytic reparameterization (Depth-muP: per-layer scale factors on weights/activities/learning rates derived from depth and width at initialization), not a dynamically measured, re-estimated-during-training precision.
why: Uses almost exactly the claim's diagnostic quantity -- an eigenvalue/spectral-norm characterization of a Jacobian-related operator (the inference Hessian, which for a PC energy is built from J^T J-like terms) to explain why plain PC fails at depth. But the fix is a fixed, closed-form, depth/width-indexed parameter rescaling chosen once at initialization, not a per-block precision re-measured from lambda_max(J^T J) of the output during training; no transformers/attention are studied.

title: ePC: Fast and Deep Predictive Coding in Digital Simulation
venue: arXiv preprint (project context identifies as accepted ICML 2026)
setting: Deep PC networks (MLP/CNN); reparameterizes inference to use errors, not activities, as the free variables
what_it_shows: Diagnoses exponential decay of the error signal with depth under standard (unit-precision) PC inference and fixes it by using error-space (not activity-space) variables integrated via reverse-mode automatic differentiation, which removes the need for any precision-matrix retuning; this is the ePC baseline already used as a comparison arm in the current study.
why: Same failure mode diagnosis as the claim (unit-precision PC does not let error reach lower layers at depth) but the fix is an entirely different mechanism class -- a change of inference variables / use of autodiff, not precision weighting from a measured Jacobian quantity -- and no transformer/attention study.

title: PredProp: Bidirectional Stochastic Optimization with Precision Weighted Predictive Coding
setting: Small CNNs/MLPs; precision matrices learned jointly with weights via gradient descent inside PC inference
what_it_shows: Learns per-unit precision (and covariance) end-to-end by gradient descent on the same free-energy objective used for weights, improving robustness/noise-handling; not tied to a measured output-Jacobian quantity and not studied for depth failure in deep transformers.
why: Shows precision CAN be learned jointly with weights in PC (so 'learnable precision' per se is known), but the specific rule (precision = measured lambda_max(J^T J) of output Jacobian, per block) and the deep-transformer training-failure motivation are absent.

title: Predictive coding, precision and natural gradients
setting: Small-scale PC networks; connects precision-weighted PC updates to natural-gradient descent
what_it_shows: Argues precision-weighted PC inference approximates natural-gradient descent on the energy, giving a theoretical account of why precision weighting improves conditioning of the update, but does not propose measuring precision from the output Jacobian's spectral norm or apply this to deep transformers.
why: Theoretical link between precision and curvature/conditioning is conceptually adjacent (precision as a curvature proxy) but the claim's concrete measured-lambda_max-per-block rule and depth-failure fix for transformers are not in this paper.

title: A theory of cortical responses
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
setting: Theoretical neuroscience; hierarchical predictive coding in cortex (no deep nets, no transformers)
what_it_shows: Introduces precision as the inverse-variance weighting of prediction errors in hierarchical predictive coding, identified with synaptic gain/attention; precision governs how much an error influences units above it.
why: Founds the general concept 'precision weights prediction errors' that the claim specializes, but has nothing about measuring precision from an output Jacobian, nothing about depth/transformers/training deep nets.

title: Understanding Sample Efficiency in Predictive Coding
setting: Deep linear networks (and non-linear extensions), analytic + empirical comparison of PC vs BP weight updates via a 'target alignment' metric.
what_it_shows: Derives closed-form expressions showing PC's weight updates move the output less 'off target' (less interference, higher cosine alignment with the training error direction) than BP's updates, especially in deep/narrow/pre-trained networks; explains PC's sample efficiency.
why: This is the closest methodological analogue found: it decomposes how much a weight update moves the output along a SPECIFIC reference direction (here, the training-error direction) versus other directions, for PC vs BP — structurally similar to the target claim's 'moves less along the directions noise pushes the input'. But the reference direction and regime are different (training-time error-interference / sample efficiency, not test-time Gaussian-noise propagation through a frozen trained predictor), it is not expressed via input-output Jacobian singular values, and it has no output-scale-refit ablation to rule out a trivial sensitivity-scale explanation.

title: Tight Stability, Convergence, and Robustness Bounds for Predictive Coding Networks
setting: Theoretical (Lyapunov/dynamical-systems analysis of PC's inference+weight dynamics); no empirical input-noise experiment.
what_it_shows: Proves PC's energy-minimizing inference dynamics are Lyapunov stable under mild assumptions, implying intrinsic robustness to small perturbations in weights/activity trajectories, and that PC weight updates approximate quasi-Newton (curvature-aware) steps.
why: Establishes a theoretical robustness property of PC, but the perturbations are to PC's own internal inference/weight dynamics, not Gaussian corruption of the external input to a trained feedforward predictor; no top-singular-value measurement, no directional (worst-case vs typical-noise-direction) decomposition, no output-rescale ablation.

title: On the role of feedback in visual processing: a predictive coding perspective (journal version: 'On the role of feedback in image recognition under noise and adversarial attacks')
setting: CNNs with trainable top-down PC feedback connections tested under pixel noise and adversarial attacks on image recognition.
what_it_shows: Predictive feedback connections trained to reconstruct lower-layer activity reduce the accuracy drop under noisy/adversarial input relative to feedforward-only CNNs, and the benefit is largest precisely under noisy conditions.
why: Directly tests noise/adversarial robustness and attributes the effect to feedback-driven denoising dynamics, but does not compare PC as a competing weight-update rule against BP at matched learning rate, does not measure or decompose Jacobian singular values, and does not run the output-scale-refit control that isolates 'moves less along the real noise direction' from 'is just less sensitive overall'.

title: Predify: Augmenting deep neural networks with brain-inspired predictive coding dynamics
setting: CNN image classifiers (feedforward, BP-trained) augmented post hoc with PC-style recurrent generative feedback loops; tested on CIFAR/noise and adversarial corruptions.
what_it_shows: Adding iterative PC feedback (an inference-time denoising mechanism layered on a conventionally-trained backbone) measurably improves robustness to additive noise and some adversarial perturbations relative to the feedforward-only network.
why: Shows a PC mechanism improves input-noise robustness, matching the qualitative phenomenon, but PC here is a test-time iterative-inference add-on over BP-trained weights, not an alternative WEIGHT learning rule trained at a matched learning rate; no Jacobian top-singular-value comparison, no decomposition of worst-case vs actual-noise-direction sensitivity, no output-scale-refit ablation.

title: Neural Networks with Recurrent Generative Feedback (CNN-F)
setting: CNN classifiers augmented with a generative feedback loop enforcing self-consistency (MAP estimation) with an internal generative model; evaluated under additive noise and adversarial perturbations.
what_it_shows: Enforcing self-consistency via recurrent generative feedback (a PC-like Bayesian-brain mechanism) improves robustness of CNNs to input noise and adversarial attacks versus the feedforward baseline.
why: Same category as Predify/feedback papers above: a PC-flavoured inference-time mechanism improves noise/adversarial robustness of an otherwise BP-trained network. No comparison of PC vs BP as competing WEIGHT learning rules, no worst-case-singular-value vs typical-direction decomposition, no output-rescale ablation.

title: Iterative VAE as a predictive brain model for out-of-distribution generalization
setting: VAEs with iterative (PC-like) inference, tested for generalization to out-of-distribution image corruptions (noise, blur, contrast, etc.).
what_it_shows: Adding iterative, PC-motivated inference on top of a VAE improves generalization/robustness to distributional image corruptions relative to a standard (non-iterative) VAE.
why: Shows a PC-like iterative-inference mechanism helps under corrupted/OOD input, paralleling the qualitative phenomenon in the claim, but again the mechanism is iterative test-time inference layered on a generative model, not a PC-vs-BP weight-learning-rule comparison at matched learning rate, and there is no Jacobian singular-value or directional-sensitivity decomposition.

title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness
setting: General (non-PC) normalized deep networks; theoretical/empirical analysis of worst-case Lipschitz constant vs. sensitivity restricted to directions within the data manifold.
what_it_shows: The worst-case (global) Lipschitz constant of normalized networks can be far larger than the network's typical sensitivity to perturbations that remain within the data's natural subspace, i.e. worst-case and on-manifold sensitivity can diverge sharply.
why: Provides the closest general-ML precedent for the worst-case-vs-typical-direction decomposition structure used in the claim (worst-case top singular value vs. sensitivity to the directions real/natural perturbations actually occupy), but is entirely about normalization layers in BP-trained networks and has no PC-vs-BP comparison.

title: Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation
setting: Theory/simulation; introduces inference-before-plasticity (iPC) as the PC learning algorithm family our ePC/PC-ALM baselines build on.
what_it_shows: Formalizes PC as a two-phase (infer activity, then update weights) algorithm and shows it approximates BP under conditions; foundational method paper, not a robustness study.
why: Defines the PC learning-rule family being compared to BP in the target paper, but contains no noise-corruption experiments, no Jacobian/sensitivity analysis, and no BP-vs-PC robustness comparison.

title: Understanding Predictive Coding as an Adaptive Trust-Region Method
setting: Theoretical analysis of PC's learning dynamics as interpolating between BP's gradient step and a second-order trust-region step.
what_it_shows: PC's weight updates can be framed as an adaptive trust-region method that incorporates curvature information, which is argued to make learning more stable than plain BP.
why: Offers a curvature/second-order account of why PC training dynamics might be more stable than BP, conceptually adjacent to 'why would PC behave differently under perturbation', but is about optimisation stability of the WEIGHT trajectory during training, not about the robustness of the trained predictor's forward map to Gaussian input noise, and has no Jacobian-direction decomposition.

title: Sparse deep predictive coding captures contour integration capabilities of the early visual system
setting: Sparse PC model of V1-like contour integration; compared against classical sparse-coding models on perceptual phenomena.
what_it_shows: A sparse predictive-coding model reproduces contour-integration illusions/robustness phenomena observed in biological vision.
why: Studies perceptual robustness qualitatively in a sparse-coding/PC model but is not a BP-vs-PC learning-rule comparison and has no Jacobian or noise-direction analysis.

title: Robust Learning with Jacobian Regularization
setting: General (non-PC) deep classifiers; regularizes the Frobenius norm of the input-output Jacobian during BP training.
what_it_shows: Penalizing the (average-case, Frobenius-norm) Jacobian during standard BP training improves robustness to input corruption and adversarial perturbations, under the premise that smaller overall sensitivity means more robustness.
why: Supplies the generic-ML intuition (lower Jacobian norm/sensitivity -> more robust) that the claim's finding runs against: here PC is reported to have a LARGER worst-case top singular value yet be more robust, because of directional alignment rather than overall magnitude. This paper never considers PC, never separates worst-case (top singular value) from the real-noise direction, and never includes an output-rescale control.

title: Deep Predictive Coding Network for Object Recognition
setting: Bi-directional recurrent PCN (feedforward + feedback + recurrent) for object recognition on natural images.
what_it_shows: A PC-style architecture with feedback/recurrent connections that iteratively reduces prediction error improves object-recognition accuracy and is discussed as plausibly more robust, but systematic noise-robustness benchmarking against a matched BP baseline is not the focus.
why: General PCN architecture background cited by the task; does not run a controlled BP-vs-PC noise-robustness comparison or any Jacobian/sensitivity analysis.

title: Sensitivity and Generalization in Neural Networks: an Empirical Study
setting: General (non-PC) deep networks trained by BP; studies input-output Jacobian norm across the input manifold as a function of training.
what_it_shows: Lower average/typical input-output sensitivity (Jacobian norm on the data manifold) correlates with better generalization across a range of architectures and training regimes.
why: General background linking Jacobian-based sensitivity to generalization/robustness in BP-trained nets; does not involve PC, does not separate worst-case from real-perturbation-direction sensitivity, and is silent on learning-rule comparisons.

title: Deep Predictive Coding Networks for Video Prediction and Unsupervised Learning (PredNet)
setting: Recurrent PC-inspired video-prediction network trained with backprop-through-time (self-supervised next-frame prediction); downstream studies probe its robustness/generalization.
what_it_shows: PredNet's feedforward+feedback+error-unit architecture (inspired by PC) learns representations useful for downstream tasks; later works probe its behaviour under distributional shift, but PredNet itself is trained by standard backprop, not PC as a weight-update rule.
why: Background/context only — PredNet borrows PC's architectural motifs but is trained by BP, so it cannot speak to a PC-vs-BP learning-rule robustness comparison; no Jacobian-direction decomposition appears in this or the robustness follow-ups found.

title: Biological Plausibility and Representational Alignment of Feedback Alignment in Convolutional Networks
setting: CNN on CIFAR-10, five learning algorithms including modified Feedback Alignment (FA) and standard BP
what_it_shows: Representational-alignment analysis (CKA-style) finds that modified FA algorithms converge on internal representations structurally SIMILAR to BP's, suggesting FA's performance comes from mimicking BP's representational geometry despite a fundamentally different weight-update rule.
why: Same analytical question as Claim 3 (does a biologically-plausible alternative to BP produce BP-like internal representations?), applied to a different alternative rule (FA, not PC) in CNNs. It reports the OPPOSITE qualitative finding to the claim (convergence to BP-like representations, not divergence in the middle with re-convergence near the output), and has no Transformer/attention component.

title: A Study of Hidden-State Optimization Order in Predictive Coding Networks
setting: MLP and mu-parametrized MLP on MNIST/CIFAR-10; standard PC, two boundary-first PC variants, and BP
what_it_shows: Directly measures (a) cosine alignment between PC parameter updates and global-BP updates during training (all PC variants stay below 0.7 alignment, i.e. gradients are NOT near-identical to BP in this setting) and (b) initial-to-final CKA and layerwise gradient-similarity diagnostics to characterize how much PC's representations change relative to BP's, finding PC's early layers barely update while BP's do.
why: This is the closest existing PC-vs-BP comparison using both a gradient-alignment metric and a CKA-based diagnostic in the same study, directly addressing the 'do PC and BP take similar/different internal paths' question the claim raises. But its CKA is initial-vs-final within one model (not a layer-wise, cross-model PC-vs-BP representational comparison), it uses MLPs (not Transformers, no attention), and it finds LOW gradient alignment (<0.7) between PC and BP rather than the near-identical (cosine ~0.99) gradients the claim reports -- a materially different gradient-similarity regime, plausibly because this uses error-propagating 'standard' PC rather than an augmented-Lagrangian/error-as-free-variable PC-ALM variant tuned to match BP more closely.

title: Uncovering the Representation of Spiking Neural Networks Trained with Surrogate Gradient
setting: ResNet-20/38/56/110/164 image classifiers on CIFAR-10; SNN (surrogate-gradient, temporal spiking) vs ANN (standard BP), same topology
what_it_shows: Cross-model, layer-by-layer CKA between an SNN and a topologically identical ANN shows a checkerboard/jagged pattern: middle-to-deep layers diverge substantially (CKA<0.2 in places) while residual-connection junctions restore similarity close to 1, even though final accuracy gaps are small (0.05-1.4 pts).
why: Methodologically the closest precedent to Claim 3's core analysis: diagonal/heatmap CKA between two differently-trained, same-topology networks, showing middle-layer divergence with re-convergence at specific points, despite near-equal task performance. But the 'different training' here is surrogate-gradient BPTT for spiking units, not a biologically-plausible local learning rule (PC/ePC) replacing backprop, the architecture is a CNN not a Transformer, and there is no attention-locality analysis.

title: Rethinking Attention Locality in Spiking Transformers
setting: Spiking Transformers (ViT-like and hierarchical) on classification/detection/segmentation benchmarks
what_it_shows: Uses Mean Attention Distance (MAD) analysis to quantify whether existing locality-enhancement methods for spiking self-attention actually produce spatially local attention, finding that computational locality does not guarantee spatial locality across layers/architectures.
why: Supplies a precedent and quantitative methodology (mean attention distance) for characterizing attention locality in a non-standard-training Transformer variant, directly relevant as a measurement-technique reference for the claim's 'PC's attention is less local' finding. But it is about spiking self-attention architecture choices under standard (surrogate-gradient) training, not about a biologically-plausible learning RULE (PC) changing attention locality relative to BP on an otherwise identical architecture.

title: Counter-Current Learning: A Biologically Plausible Dual Network Approach for Deep Learning
setting: MLP/CNN on MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10/100; dual forward+feedback network trained without end-to-end BP
what_it_shows: Uses Centered Kernel Alignment (citing Kornblith et al. 2019) to track representational similarity BETWEEN the forward and feedback sub-networks of its own dual-network scheme over training, finding they progressively align at high layers (a 'counter-current' reciprocal structure).
why: Applies the same CKA methodology to a biologically-plausible learning scheme, but the two things being compared are two halves of one non-BP model (forward vs. feedback pathway), not a non-BP-trained network vs. a separately BP-trained network of the same architecture. No Transformer attention analysis.

title: Towards Biologically Plausible Computing: A Comprehensive Comparison
setting: MLP/CNN on MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, nine bio-plausible algorithms (incl. predictive coding, feedback alignment, target propagation, forward-forward, Hebbian, STDP, equilibrium propagation, local losses) vs BP
what_it_shows: Benchmarks accuracy of each rule vs BP, and separately computes Representational Dissimilarity Matrix (RDM) similarity between each algorithm's learned features and human fMRI/EEG brain activity (Haxby dataset) -- finding PC's brain-RDM similarity (0.805-0.806) is actually slightly higher than BP's (0.799-0.795).
why: Includes predictive coding as one of several BP alternatives and performs a representational-similarity analysis, but the similarity target is brain activity (RSA/RDM to fMRI), not a layer-wise or cross-model comparison of PC's internal representations against BP's own representations. No CKA between PC and BP networks directly, no Transformer, no attention-locality analysis.

title: On the relationship between predictive coding and backpropagation
setting: MLPs/CNNs, theoretical + empirical comparison of predictive-coding and backpropagation gradients
what_it_shows: Shows (building on Whittington & Bogacz 2017 and Millidge et al.) that predictive coding's weight updates converge to the exact backpropagation gradient at the inference fixed point, i.e. PC and BP compute near-identical gradients under the right conditions.
why: Establishes as prior, well-known theory/empirics the first half of the claim -- that PC and BP can produce near-identical gradients during training -- but says nothing about whether the resulting hidden-layer representations or attention patterns then diverge; no CKA, no Transformer, no attention analysis.

title: Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited
setting: CNNs/ResNets, various architectures, same training algorithm (BP) at different widths/depths/seeds
what_it_shows: Introduces (linear) CKA as a representational-similarity metric robust to invertible linear transforms and isotropic scaling, and uses it to compare layers within and across BP-trained networks (e.g. across random seeds, widths).
why: This is the method itself (CKA) that the claim applies to compare PC vs BP transformers. It establishes CKA as the standard tool and reports CKA ~0.99+ between BP seeds as the normal 'same-solution' baseline, which the claim's BP-BP CKA (0.98-0.99) reproduces, but it never compares BP to a non-BP learning rule or to attention patterns.

title: Understanding Sample Efficiency in Predictive Coding
setting: deep linear and nonlinear networks, PC vs BP, 'target alignment' metric
what_it_shows: Derives exact target-alignment expressions in deep linear networks showing PC's learning efficiency advantage over BP is 'especially pronounced in deep, narrow and pre-trained networks', i.e. a depth-dependent PC-BP gap in learning efficiency.
why: Directly shows a depth-dependent PC-vs-BP difference in learning dynamics (target alignment), structurally analogous to 'greater depth halves the gap', but the quantity analysed is scalar target-alignment/sample efficiency, not a principal-component-resolved regression slope of residual error against target variance.

title: Towards Scaling Deep Neural Networks with Predictive Coding: Theory and Practice (PhD thesis)
setting: theoretical analysis of PC inference/learning dynamics, PCN scaling
what_it_shows: Proves PC's learning dynamics are an approximate trust-region method using second-order (Gauss-Newton-like) information despite using only local first-order updates, and studies how this reshapes the effective loss landscape PC descends.
why: This is exactly the 'PC as trust-region/Gauss-Newton' theoretical mechanism the claim's search brief points to -- a plausible cause for PC treating different error-covariance directions differently from BP -- but the thesis never measures a regression slope of PC's error against target-PC-space variance, nor a depth-dependent fine-detail gap; those remain untested empirical predictions.

title: Only Strict Saddles in the Energy Landscape of Predictive Coding Networks?
setting: deep linear and nonlinear PC networks, equilibrated energy landscape analysis
what_it_shows: Shows PC's inference equilibrium rescales the MSE loss in a weight-dependent way that removes many degenerate (non-strict) saddles, making the effective landscape PC trains on different in curvature from the raw BP loss.
why: Establishes that PC's effective loss landscape has different, weight-dependent curvature from BP's MSE landscape -- a mechanism that could plausibly reweight learning of different error directions -- but never decomposes residual error by target principal component/variance, and draws no claim about depth and a fine-detail gap.

title: Understanding and Improving Optimization in Predictive Coding Networks
setting: PC networks (IL) vs BP, convergence-speed analysis
what_it_shows: Establishes theoretical conditions under which IL is sensitive to second- and higher-order curvature information, and shows IL can reduce loss faster than BP in some regimes.
why: Further develops the curvature-sensitivity account of why PC and BP differ in convergence, consistent with (but not testing) a spectral reweighting of learning; no principal-component error decomposition or depth-halving result is reported.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Inference Learning
setting: deep (non-)linear networks trained with PC inference learning (IL) vs BP
what_it_shows: Shows IL (PC's inference learning) closely approximates implicit SGD, a distinct optimisation method from BP's explicit SGD, explaining IL's improved stability across learning rates and faster small-batch convergence.
why: Gives a mechanistic reason (implicit vs explicit SGD) why PC and BP trajectories differ, which is complementary to the trust-region account and could underlie a differential treatment of error directions, but the paper never analyses the spectral/principal-component content of the residual difference, nor depth effects on it.

title: Deep Frequency Principle: Towards Understanding Why Deeper Learning Is Faster
setting: BP-trained feedforward networks of varying depth, Fourier-analyzed by layer
what_it_shows: Shows empirically that as effective depth increases (via composition of hidden layers), the F-Principle (low-frequency-first bias) becomes stronger/faster at a given layer, i.e. depth changes the spectral-bias dynamics quantitatively.
why: This is the closest existing precedent for 'depth modulates a spectral-bias gap', but entirely within BP (no PC/local-rule comparison) and about within-training-trajectory frequency dynamics, not a fixed PC-vs-BP fine-detail gap that halves with depth.

title: Exact Solutions to the Nonlinear Dynamics of Learning in Deep Linear Neural Networks
setting: deep linear networks trained by gradient descent on linear regression tasks
what_it_shows: Derives exact learning-dynamics solutions showing that singular-value (principal) modes of the input-output correlation are learned in order of decreasing singular value magnitude, i.e. high-variance modes are fit before low-variance/fine modes, under ordinary gradient descent.
why: This is the canonical result behind 'principal-component-ordered learning' that the claim's framing of a BP baseline rests on, but it concerns one learning rule (gradient descent / effectively BP) and deep *linear* nets; it makes no PC-vs-BP comparison and no depth-halves-the-residual-gap statement.

title: mu-PC: Scaling Predictive Coding to 100+ Layer Networks
setting: deep (up to 128-layer) residual PC networks, depth-mu-parameterisation
what_it_shows: Identifies depth-dependent pathologies in standard PC training and shows a parameterisation that stabilizes PC learning rates/performance across depths 1-128.
why: Studies how PC's trainability and performance change with depth, but measures aggregate task accuracy/stability, not a spectral or principal-component decomposition of the PC-BP residual error.

title: From Lazy to Rich: Exact Learning Dynamics in Deep Linear Networks
setting: deep linear networks, lambda-balanced initializations, GD training
what_it_shows: Derives exact solutions for how initialization scale moves learning between lazy (static representation) and rich (evolving, feature-learning) regimes, including how this affects mode-wise learning dynamics.
why: Further develops the deep-linear-network mode-dynamics toolkit the claim's PC analysis would need, but addresses GD regime (lazy/rich), not PC vs BP or depth-dependent fine-detail gaps.

title: Align, Then Memorise: the Dynamics of Learning with Feedback Alignment
setting: deep linear and nonlinear networks trained with Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), a different biologically-plausible local learning rule
what_it_shows: Shows DFA learning proceeds in a layer-ordered alignment-then-memorisation sequence and that convergence depends on the conditioning of layer-wise alignment matrices, i.e. a different, non-BP rule has its own structured order/bottleneck in what it learns first.
why: Demonstrates that a different bio-plausible local rule (DFA, not PC) has its own mode/order-dependent learning dynamics distinct from BP, supporting the general idea that local rules can show rule-specific spectral/structural biases, but is not about PC and not about principal-component/frequency content specifically.

title: On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks
setting: BP-trained MLPs/CNNs fit synthetic & real regression/classification targets
what_it_shows: Establishes empirically and via NTK eigenspectrum theory that BP-trained networks learn low-frequency (high-eigenvalue) target components first and higher-frequency (fine) components slower.
why: Defines the spectral-bias phenomenon for BP itself; says nothing about PC or about a PC-vs-BP gap, but is the conceptual ancestor of the claim's framing.

title: Frequency Principle: Fourier Analysis Sheds Light on Deep Neural Networks
setting: DNNs (incl. VGG16) on MNIST/CIFAR-10 trained by SGD
what_it_shows: Empirically demonstrates the F-Principle: networks fit target functions from low to high frequency during BP training, on image benchmarks including CIFAR-10.
why: Same CIFAR-10-style setting and 'low frequencies learned first' phenomenon as the claim, but purely about standard BP/SGD, no PC or local-learning comparison, no depth-dependence-of-gap result.

title: Theory of the Frequency Principle for General Deep Neural Networks
setting: theoretical analysis of general DNN training
what_it_shows: Provides a theoretical account (NTK-based) of why and how strongly the F-Principle/spectral bias holds for general deep networks.
why: Theoretical grounding for spectral bias in BP networks; no PC, no depth-halves-the-gap result.

title: A Mathematical Theory of Semantic Development in Deep Neural Networks
setting: deep linear networks learning hierarchical/semantic structure
what_it_shows: Extends the singular-mode learning-dynamics theory to explain staged acquisition of coarse-to-fine semantic structure, again ordered by the singular value/variance of each mode under gradient descent.
why: Reinforces the coarse-before-fine/high-variance-before-low-variance ordering for BP-style learning, but not about PC or about a residual PC-BP gap.

title: High-Dimensional Dynamics of Generalization Error in Neural Networks
setting: large linear/shallow nonlinear networks, random matrix theory analysis
what_it_shows: Shows generalization error dynamics are governed by eigenmode-specific learning timescales set by the data covariance spectrum, under ordinary GD training.
why: Further confirms mode-dependent (variance-ordered) learning speed as a generic GD phenomenon; no PC, no fine-detail-regression-slope or depth-halving result.
